en: Preface:
To recite the Buddha’s name in every thought—reciting him as he truly is—is what is called the Amitābha of Self-Nature.

To visualize the Western Quarter while relying on correct contemplation is what is called the Pure Land of Mind-Only. As it is said: "According to the purity of one's mind, so is the purity of the Buddha-land."
It is so, it is so. All sentient beings are entirely deluded regarding their true nature; where is Amitābha? Their whole minds pursue external objects;
where does the Pure Land exist? Although they possess the virtues of their nature, they have not yet undergone cultivation and refinement, being buried by the three subtle and six coarse [delusions].
Having been oblivious to the jewel within one's own garment, one wanders through the six realms of existence; the Tathāgata regards such a person as truly pitiable.

Even worldly wealth and status, the meritorious rewards of humans and devas, require diligent toil and are difficult to satisfy the mind; how much more so is this the case for transcending the world and attaining liberation from birth and death?
Having already given rise to hope, yet fearing the diligent cultivation [of the path], they speak empty words of the nature of virtue, deceiving themselves and others.
When the thirtieth day of the twelfth lunar month arrives, what can be done to remedy their regret?

As for those who have faith in this gate and are willing to practice it, yet upon seeing even a small portion of the *Sūtras*, they immediately give rise to distorted views—such people are indeed numerous. During the time of Tiantai, he already discussed the "Ten Doubts"; as for our Master...
Zi Lin, furthermore, I ask: in this age of semblance and the final dharma, obstacles and afflictions are so numerous.

Having received the Buddha’s secret entrustment, the great bodhisattvas have, according to the times, opened the way and, according to capacities, provided healing. Zhi Zhe and Tian Ru were both such individuals.

Yet even now, after several hundred more years have passed, our roots of goodness have become increasingly thin while obstacles and attachments grow ever stronger; though one might occasionally resolve to practice, it is difficult to encounter [such teachers].

The Venerable Shandao was a water-and-cloud practitioner who profoundly plumbed the ocean of the teachings; his principles encompassed the three schools of doctrine and he directly penetrated the source of Chan, his lamp illuminating all five branches.
He guided beings of the three capacities by solely propagating the Pure Land. His immediate method followed that of Xing’an, while his distant lineage honored that of Yunqi.
Thus, there already existed the expositions of the nine patriarchs; now, with its universal applicability and its simultaneous integration of doctrine and practice, it is suitable for beginners.

Indeed! Long cultivation must surely follow this path. This single fascicle of the *One Hundred Questions on the Buddha-Recitation* is sweet from beginning to end and penetrating from start to finish.

It is both concise and comprehensive, as well as profound yet accessible. It sweeps away the doctrine of "mind-only" and does not speak of "self-nature," ultimately recognizing the provisional vehicle rather than clinging to the ultimate reality.
Furthermore, it is something that the venerable masters of antiquity have never before expounded. Why is this? Because of [their] attachment...
Those who rely on intellectual reasoning often neglect actual practice and, conversely, err by seeking rebirth in the West;

those who cling to phenomenal appearances do not abandon conditioned existence, yet they recognize this unimpeded direct path as a provisional teaching or a mere expedient device. This shortcut within shortcuts clearly reveals the Buddha’s compassion and makes his guidance most intimate and personal.
Such an instruction is truly the precious raft of the Lotus School and the ultimate destination for the Pure Land—spoken from the very mouth [of the Master].

It is exhausted; not even a single character remains. If readers can truly attain joy in their hearts and sincere submission, then as for the diligence described, the Compassionate Honored One will certainly provide remote protection and acceptance.
Within the pond of eight virtues, a lotus flower shall surely bloom. When the spirit transforms and the form migrates, one will certainly find a place of rebirth.
May I, this man of the Way, testify that this is not false. This junior student of the final age, having washed his hands and burned incense, bows his head...
I have reverently read this work and offer praise without end. Regarding the *Ten Doubts* and the *Oral Questions*, these are the true transmission of the "Droplets of Marrow" from Master Lianchi.

It is so, it is so. Wherever this book resides, the Buddhas and Patriarchs will protect and mind it. Those with the karmic affinity to encounter it should cause it to be widely circulated and scatter various incense and flowers as an offering to it.
Preface Written by the Student of Pure Practice, Jiang Yuan, on the First Day of the Second Month of Winter in the Fifth Year of the Daoguang Reign.

Regarding the title *One Hundred Questions on Buddha-Recitation*: Where there is a question, there must be an answer. As for the fact that "answers" is not explicitly stated [in the title], it is because the answers are subsumed within them.

Regarding the "Questions": this is an abbreviation for what would have been several hundred questions; since all that was discussed concerned the practice of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation), it is titled the "Hundred Questions on Buddha-Recitation.
Someone asked: "Was it indeed those who questioned and you who answered? I reflected for a long time and said:
"Although these [questions] emerged from my own side, I only know that they all discuss the matter of Buddha-recitation; I no longer remember [the specific details]."
In this matter, it may be that I asked and he answered, or that he asked and I answered.
Although both he and I were at a loss and knew nothing of it, the matters of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation) we discussed remain vividly present here.

I request those practitioners of pure karma who apply their minds to *nien-fo* to contemplate and reflect upon this; perhaps it may serve as a small contribution, like the light of a firefly. Thus it is said:
Completed.
Written on the first day of the sixth month of summer in the year of Yisi (4859), the fifth year of the Daoguang era, by the junior scholar Wukai of Gusu.
Four prefaces to the rules.

This work is primarily intended for lay practitioners of the Buddha-remembrance (nienfo). It seeks to reach directly to the source of the mind and thoroughly sweeps away fragmented and circuitous approaches.
May those good-hearted students of the Way apply themselves to its contemplation; meanwhile, I, too, shall use it as a means of self-exhortation.
These remarks concern only the immediate moment; they aim solely for clarity and lucidity rather than extensive exposition.
As these are spoken specifically for laypeople, I consider my own virtue to be meager and do not dare to presumptuously trouble my fellow practitioners with them.
Nevertheless, there may be points herein that admit of interpretation;

I pray that the discerning scholars among the eminent practitioners will deign to grant me their instruction. As for any errors or fallacies within this work, I would be most grateful for your correction and rectification.
One Hundred Questions on the Buddha-Recitation:
Composed by the junior monk Wukai of Lianhua Hermitage in Qingyunjian.
Regarding the Pure Land Dharma Gate: How is it that one speaks correctly without falling into partiality or deviation? (1)
This gateway of the Dharma path encompasses all capacities and dispositions equally. As for its institutional arrangements, it is fitting that they reach both the highest and the lowest;
they fully include all five teachings. Reaching upward, they serve those of superior faculties; reaching downward, they accommodate those of inferior faculties.

Faith, practice, and vows constitute what are known as the provisions (*sambhāra*). The Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma all serve as auxiliary practices. In their ultimate convergence, none can be separated from purity.
The three sutras on the Pure Land establish the teaching in this manner; this is called the correct teaching.
From antiquity to the present, who among the great spiritual benefactors (*mahāsattva*) of the Eastern Land has propagated this correct teaching on the practice of purity? (2)
There are two types of "correct exposition" (*samyag-deśanā*). First is the "correct exposition of the universal path," which is the totality of the great function.

Second is the "correct exposition that accords with the capacities of beings," which addresses specific phenomena and principles. Great spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) of antiquity and today are beyond counting;

their writings have for the most part been lost or scattered. Among those currently extant, my humble self has read very little. Relying solely on what I have seen and heard, [I shall discuss] Yunqi Mi...
The *Tōsho Shō* (Commentary on the Tōsho) represents the great function of the entire body [of the Buddha-nature] and constitutes the standard, orthodox teaching.

Works such as Tiantai’s *Ten Doubts* and Tianru’s *Huowen* all address specific matters and principles as direct teachings suited to particular capacities; they are of the utmost importance for practitioners of the Pure Land path.
One must by all means seek to read and contemplate it with relish.

The *Miaozongchao* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning) uses the three contemplations (*sanguan*) to provide an explanation; because those of dull faculties find it difficult to enter, is that not also a partial teaching? (3)
The Dharma is profound, deep, subtle, and far-reaching; were it not for the Three Contemplations of Tiantai, its perfect and wondrous nature could not be fully revealed.
This is the definitive teaching, not a partial one. For those of dull faculties who find entry difficult, they may recite the *Contemplation Sutra* extensively.

By becoming thoroughly familiar with its recitation and its contemplation, and by visualizing according to the text of the sutra, although they may not yet open their wisdom-nature or achieve the path of contemplation, [they will still attain benefit].
This is but a single method for those of coarse and shallow learning. It requires only the recitation and visualization of the *Amitābha Sūtra*;
one must not add a single word of personal interpretation beyond what is in the sūtra. One must remain strictly within the text and refrain from arbitrary or speculative discourse.
Should you fail to follow these instructions, I fear you will fall into the influence of demonic delusions.
4. How far apart are the perfect subtlety of contemplative visualization and the single-mindedness of principle achieved through the recitation of the name?
They are both equally inconceivable.
5. In the lower grade of the *Contemplation Sutra*, one attains rebirth through the recitation of the name; to what realm does such recitation lead?
If one reaches the state of *shishi-ichinen* (the single-mindedness of the phenomenal), one will attain rebirth; if one does not reach *shishi-ichinen*, can one still attain rebirth?
(6) It is difficult to attain rebirth without reaching *shishi-ichinen*. How is this known? The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* says: "With a single mind..."
Without confusion, at the time when that person approaches the end of life, Amitābha Buddha, together with the assembly of holy beings, will appear before them.
At the moment of death, this person’s mind will not be inverted, and they will immediately attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitābha Buddha.

The mind is not inverted; it is single-minded and undistracted. Although one may not yet be able to achieve the principle of single-mindedness (*li-yixin*), it is quite clear that one must at least practice the practice of single-mindedness (*shi-yixin*).
When reciting the Buddha’s name, if there are generally various distracting thoughts, how can one be single-minded? (7)
If you are willing to read the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* extensively and practice meditative reflection, you will surely gradually attain single-mindedness (*ekacitta*).
The *Contemplation Sūtra* states: "Those who wish to be born in that land should cultivate the three types of merit.
It further states: "These three matters are called pure karma (*śukla-karman*. And it says again: "These three kinds of karma pertain to the three periods of time—past, future, and present."
"The Buddhas are the true cause for pure karma. Based on this, they are already the true cause for pure karma;
is it not unnecessary to further seek out contemplative methods? (8)

The primary purport of this sutra lies in the sixteen contemplation gates. What is called "the correct cause for pure karma" refers precisely to the "correct" within the distinction between the partial and the correct;

it is not the "correct" as opposed to the auxiliary. This is like saying that these three types of merit are the truly correct causes among the practices for pure karma, rather than being partial or deviant causes.
The *Contemplation Sūtra* states: "It is this mind that creates the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha. What is the meaning of this?
(9) "Creator" refers to cultivation. It means that this mind cultivates the Buddha-way, and this mind is fundamentally the Buddha.
Since one is fundamentally a Buddha, why rely on cultivation? Therefore, to be without mind is to be in accord with the Way; the Way resides therein.
To give rise to thoughts and engage in cultivation only serves to nourish delusion (10).
If one does not cultivate until reaching the stage of perfection, how can one attain the state of mindlessness that accords with the Way? Is the Way truly found therein?

To cultivate while increasing delusion, or to achieve cultivation only for the extinction of delusion—these are both flawed. Not to cultivate yet still harbor delusion leads to an endless succession of delusions. Reflect upon this.
The *Contemplation Sūtra* states: "In this very life, one attains the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (*nien-fo san-mei*). What is meant by "Buddha-remembrance samādhi"?

(11) The Sanskrit term *samādhi* is translated here as "right concentration" (*zheng-ding*) and also as "right reception" (*zheng-shou*). As for Buddha-remembrance samādhi, it refers to focused thought and visualization.

Ji: "Wisdom and principle are in profound accord. Desiring that people may easily understand, I shall provide another explanation: mindfulness is itself the Buddha, and the Buddha is itself mindfulness.
Mindfulness of the Buddha is a single suchness, and therein not even the mark of 'mindfulness of the Buddha' can be apprehended. This is called the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha."
Regarding the visualization of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*: his body is sixty million billion nayuta Ganges-sands of yojanas in height.
What is the method for this visualization? (12)
Self and other are mutually extinguished; one contemplates according to what has been taught.
As stated in the *Commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra*, why is this called the "General Correct Teaching" (13)?

It is because it is neither artificial nor crooked, without factionalism or partiality, being central, upright, harmonious, and peaceful; it alone clarifies the essential meaning, and thus it is termed "general."
The Correct Teaching:
The Ten Doubts or Questions. Why is it called the "Correct Teaching that Adapts to Capacities through One Matter and One Principle" (14)?

At the very beginning, when one wishes to give rise to faith, one still possesses doubts. The *Ten Doubts Treatise* analyzes and clarifies the reasons for this, causing one to suddenly attain enlightenment and be free from them.

[Obstruction]. Those who practice Chan meditation, upon gaining even a slight understanding of "light and shadow," often treat the Lotus School with contempt; this is entirely due to their failure to comprehend the Buddha’s principles, leading them mistakenly into madness and delusion.
Master Tianru struck the gong with great force to shatter the net of confusion, specifically for the sake of a certain class of practitioners, to reveal the correct purport.
He termed this "one matter and one principle" as the direct teaching suited to their capacities. Of these two [approaches], the latter is...
This is of vital importance; therefore, it is specifically highlighted.
What kind of temperament must a practitioner possess to easily enter the Way? (15)
Firmness, vigor, centrality, and correctness—these qualities of character make one a fit vessel for the Dharma. Firmness enables one to shoulder the burden of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
vigor enables one to act for the sake of the Dharma and for sentient beings; centrality ensures one does not fall into deviant paths;
and correctness prevents the arising of perverse thoughts. In the past, when Linji first entered the Way, he attended upon Huangbo; Muzhou observed him...
His practice was singularly pure. When he sought the general meaning of the Buddha-dharma from Huangbo, he received the staff three times under Linji.

Immediately upon hearing the words of Dayu, he attained a thorough realization that the Buddha-dharma is not something complicated. One should know that this great enlightenment at that time arose entirely from his long-standing purity of practice;
had it not been for the purity of his practice, even if there were hundreds or thousands of Huangbos, [he would not have awakened].
"How could a fool achieve great enlightenment? Yet Linji’s conduct was pure and singular; this was also due to the purity of his innate disposition (*prakṛti*).
A Confucian text states: 'Yanzi was profound, hidden, and pure, and thus he became a preeminent disciple of the school of Confucius.

How much more so for one who is a vessel of the Dharma within the Buddhist gate—how could he be inferior to this? Among those praised throughout antiquity as great *kalyāṇamitras* in the Chan lineage..."

Mazu, Baizhang, and others; those within the teachings such as Qingliang, Tiantai, and others; and those of the Pure Land school such as the nine patriarchs of the Lotus Sect—all were individuals of resolute vigor, central rectitude, and pure integrity.
However, this is merely discussed from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and is but a limited view.
In reality, their roots of great wisdom shine with light that penetrates to the very limits of existence; how could they be described in words? I—
For those later-born youths who dare to aspire to the Great Way, how could they not exert themselves?
His gate and courtyard stand preeminent, so lofty as to be unattainable; those of shallow nature and mediocre station retreat upon seeing his precipice.
How, then, can it be said that [the teaching] universally benefits those of the three capacities? (16)
In general, when studying the Way, one must first understand the ultimate principle. It is like the Confucian practice of cultivating virtue and discussing learning:

one must first understand why Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, Wu, the Duke of Zhou, and Confucius were what they were—Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, Wu, the Duke of Zhou, and Confucius—and only then proceed to study step by step. Even if one does not become a sage, one will at least become a worthy.
One may not become a sage, yet one will certainly become a great scholar. According to the depth or shallowness of one's learning, all will remain disciples of the Gate of Sages.
Those who practice the mindfulness of the Buddha today should first understand the fundamental vow and merit of Amitābha Buddha, and further know the lofty character of the successive patriarchs;
only then should they proceed step by step. Even if one does not achieve full perfection, [one will still attain the goal].
Whether it be seven, eight, five, or six [recitations], or even one or two parts, according to the depth or shallowness of their power of study, all may be called the accomplishment of pure karma.
Once accomplished, they all attain rebirth; once reborn, they all attain non-retrogression.
All shall attain direct entry into unsurpassed bodhi. How has it ever not been that the three faculties are universally encompassed?
Those who retreat upon seeing the precipice are not fit to speak with those who possess true faith. If their faith is not genuine, even the Buddha can do nothing for them.
Even those who have achieved one or two parts [of the practice] shall all attain rebirth.

Why is it that those who have practiced sincere nianfo for twenty or thirty years rarely hear of auspicious signs at the time of their death? Is it because after such a long duration, they have still not achieved even one or two parts? (17)
This is truly because one recognizes the recitation of the Buddha’s name as something real, rather than recognizing it as something correct. Why is this?

It may be that when one is told the essential and true Dharma, because it does not accord with one's own inclinations, it does not enter one's ears; or it may be that one hears what is empty, flowery, and of no benefit.
Because it happened to coincide with my own inclinations, I immediately resolved to carry it out.

Seeking not the True Dharma, but merely following my own whims, I have thus drifted with the waves and currents, spending my entire life in restless agitation. This is what is called "carrying hemp while discarding gold," wasting one's time in vain.
If you wish to achieve the accomplishment of pure karma through even one or two parts, you should immediately apply yourself with vigorous introspection.
The ancients said that mindfulness of the Buddha does not obstruct the practice of Chan, and the practice of Chan does not obstruct mindfulness of the Buddha;
yet others have said that mindfulness of the Buddha obstructs the practice of Chan, and the practice of Chan obstructs mindfulness of the Buddha. Ultimately, which is it? (18)
The Dharma has two gates, yet its principle is not of two kinds. To point to the principle, one says there is no obstruction; to point to the phenomena (dharma), one says there is obstruction.
However, the principle becomes manifest only after awakening, whereas the phenomena are what are employed in the present moment. "Phenomena" refers to methods;

these methods are not of two types, for the mind does not have two functions—hence it is said there is obstruction. Since the source from which they return is not dual, it is said there is no obstruction.
"Those of sharp faculties should practice Chan; those of dull faculties should practice nianfo (Buddha-recitation)," is this not so?

(19) Regarding Chan and nianfo, it is appropriate for each to follow their own inclination. If one were to rigidly assign them according to sharpness or dullness, what kind of statement would that be?

If one’s will and spirit are firm and courageous, even those of dull faculties can attain enlightenment. However, investigating the essence of nianfo cannot be accomplished without sharp faculties. If one speaks of the Patriarchs...
Under the Master’s gate, he exclusively receives those of superior capacity. That "fools, both men and women, all practice mindfulness of the Buddha" is merely a general statement.

Once one has attained awakening through Zen meditation, one stands shoulder-to-shoulder with the Buddha; yet, if one merely practices mindfulness of the Buddha for rebirth in the Pure Land, one does not escape birth and death. Is this so, or not? (20)
Even after awakening, one must still await further cultivation because the flow of karmic consciousness has not yet been purified; Master Guishan spoke of this in detail.
One hears only of being born within a lotus flower in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, but one does not hear of dying within a lotus flower in the Land of Ultimate Bliss;
Master Liaochi spoke of this exhaustively. Alas! Lacking right knowledge and vision, and furthermore failing to understand...
The Ritual Code contains such errors; be cautious!
Zhongfeng said: "Chan is the Chan of the Pure Land; the Pure Land is the Pure Land of Chan. What does this mean? (21)

In Sanskrit, this is *dhyāna*; here it is translated as "meditative concentration" (*zhènglù*). That which is contemplative while being tranquil is *samādhi* (concentration); that which is tranquil while being contemplative is *prajñā* (wisdom). What is called "dhyāna" refers precisely to concentration and wisdom.
The Dharma-gate of the Pure Land also relies upon concentration and wisdom. Although the two names "dhyāna" and "Pure Land" differ, their concentration and wisdom are one and the same.
When we speak of the concentration and wisdom of the Pure Land, it is simply the concentration and wisdom of the Pure Land. The Pure Land...

"This is the pure land of concentration and wisdom. Zhongfeng’s words here are intended to urge those engaged in pure practices to advance toward the merit of concentration and wisdom, and to admonish his disciples to open the path of pure land cultivation;
they constitute a teaching on the dual cultivation of Chan and Pure Land.
The concurrent cultivation of Chan and Pure Land must be distinguished as either sequential or simultaneous (22).
The fundamental tenet of Bodhidharma transcends the vehicles of the teachings and is not the same as the four dhyānas or eight samādhis. Therefore, the ancients said:
"This [Chan] does not even accord with the vehicles of the teachings, let alone with Confucian texts. Thus, one should know that they must be distinguished as sequential; if one first engages in...

To see one's nature through Chan and yet further cultivate pure karma is most in accord with principle. That the dragons and elephants of the ancestral gate throughout antiquity all extensively propagated pure karma was precisely like this.
Cloud of Celestial Garments: "To be born is to be definitely born; to go is truly not to go. What does this mean?
(23) Regarding rebirth in the Pure Land, the Buddha’s words are never false; therefore, it is said that "to be born is to be definitely born.
If one realizes that Amitābha is one's own original nature and that the original nature is Amitābha, then the Tathāgata comes from nowhere and goes nowhere. Therefore...
To say that when clouds depart they do not truly depart is a statement that presents both principle and phenomena together, manifesting both the provisional and the ultimate simultaneously.
Regarding the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land, it is often referred to as "meditative contemplation" (dhyāna-vipaśyanā). What kind of meditation is this? (24)

This is not the Dharma-citta meditation (Dharmic Chan), nor is it the meditation of the four dhyānas or eight samādhis. What is called "meditation" here is the investigation into the essence of nianfo;

it is the method of "holding the name" through principle within the practice of recitation. When the holding of the name reaches the ultimate state of single-mindedness, this is the Dharma-citta meditation.
The four dhyānas and the eight samādhis are not two different things.

One should cultivate both dhyāna and purity together; it is appropriate to practice dhyāna first and purity afterward. I have already heard your instruction on this, but why is it that they cannot be cultivated simultaneously? Is there an explanation for this? (25)

In the practice of nianfo (buddha-recollection), one does not fear grasping at signs; in the practice of chan (seated meditation), one must first detach from signs. Grasping and detachment are difficult to practice simultaneously.
To linger in attachment and fixate on signs is to remain within delusive conditions, a point for which the wise offer their censure; this is precisely why it is so. (26)
Contemplate the name of the Perfectly Enlightened Amitābha Buddha and visualize the pure and majestic features of the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

If one remains attached in this manner, it is feared that the practice will not be truly earnest. If one can indeed be truly earnest, then the various illusory and delusive conditions of the world will naturally be left behind;
this is precisely the method for abandoning the false to return to the true, turning away from defilement to unite with reality.
This is the method for awakening. Furthermore, both grasping at signs and being free from signs are merely skillful means for entering the gate.
It is like one who wishes to reach home: if they do not enter through the door, can they still arrive?
Whenever I observe the instructions of the ancient worthies regarding the practice of nianfo (reciting the Buddha’s name), they tell one to look into who it is that is reciting;
this is similar to investigating a *huatou* (critical phrase). Furthermore, they say to ask oneself: "Which of these is the original-nature Amitābha? Such is their method. (27)
This is a modification of the Dharma by later masters; it is not the Buddha’s true intent regarding the pure practice.
While the masters’ intention was to lead people to awaken to and clarify their original nature, even the inclusion of the word "who" (誰) is questionable.

If one asks oneself, "Which of these is the original nature Amitābha?", one cannot avoid falling into the fault of allowing consciousness and emotion to settle upon the object. Lately, those acting as masters...
Those who have shifted their focus toward study are especially prone to this; true masters of the school would certainly not act in such a manner.

Students all claim that through Zen one can attain awakening, whereas through the recitation of the Buddha’s name one cannot. Thus we know that the recitation of the Buddha’s name does not equal the practice of Zen. (28)

The claim that "reciting the Buddha's name cannot lead to awakening" is the talk of a rustic from the east of Qi. The *Śūraṃgama-sūtra*, in the chapter on the Perfect Penetration of Mahāsthāmaprāpta, states:

"Without relying on expedient means, one spontaneously attains the opening of the mind. To speak of the "opening of the mind"—is this not the state of awakening? The *Amitābha Sūtra*, in the chapter on rebirth for those of superior capacity, states:
"They understand the primary meaning. To speak of "understanding the primary meaning"—is this not the state of awakening? It is the realization of the purity of the sole mind.

The "Earth" [in the title] refers to the original nature of Amitābha. To speak of "attaining" (*da*) or "realizing" (*liao*) this—how could this not be the realm of awakening? To state the essential point:

the practice of investigating the essence through *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation) is entirely the realm of awakening. This is clearly evident in the section on the "Principle of Single-Mindedness" in Yunqi’s *Commentary on the Sutra*.
It is simply that within the Pure Land Dharma-gate, while one seeks rebirth through faith and aspiration, the actual cultivation of *nien-fo* is the most vital and primary principle. Awakening...
One does not awaken; one does not calculate. Thus, Master Yongming had the discernment that says: "If one only attains the vision of Amitābha, why worry about not attaining awakening?
One should know that this was not said because of an inability to awaken due to causes and conditions.
As for the Chan school of Bodhidharma, if a student reaches the point where the bottom of the bucket falls away and further penetrates the final, secure barrier, they will become a liberated person.
Śānhànzi: The strategic methods of such people surpass all dharma-gates; therefore, it is called the Chan of the Patriarchs.
As for the four kinds of mindfulness of the Buddha, what is their teaching? (29)
The four types are: mindfulness through reciting the name, mindfulness by contemplating an image, mindfulness by contemplating the visualization, and mindfulness of the true aspect (*dharmatā*).
Contemplating an image serves to collect and concentrate the body and mind; it can act as a precursor to contemplative visualization and as an auxiliary condition for the recitation of the name.
As for the true aspect, it is the aspect that is free from all aspects. It is devoid of faults and transcends all negations; it is inconceivable. To maintain this is...

This is called the single mind that reaches the ultimate principle. When contemplation reaches the point where both vitarka (initial thought) and vicāra (sustained thought) are simultaneously extinguished, one returns to the same reality of the true mark (*dharmatā*).
This is the ultimate standard of Buddha-recitation; its divine power and wondrous function cannot be fathomed by those who possess only a superficial samādhi of mere lip-service.
The practice of Buddha-recollection (buddhānusmṛti) has long been renowned for its simplicity and ease. Why, then, do you now speak of such difficulties?
(30) There are two meanings to the term "simplicity and ease. First, it refers to those of middling and inferior capacities;

for them, the essential teaching is to sever the cycle of saṃsāra, proceed directly to the Western Land, and forever transcend birth and death, requiring nothing more than single-minded devotion to Buddha-recollection with an undistorted mind.

Regardless of whether one is wise or foolish, all are able to achieve success; therefore, it is called "simple and easy. According to the former approach, one must cultivate the six perfections and myriad practices over kalpas of aeons before attaining the Buddha-way.
Now, however, by means of the six great characters of the Name, there is no restriction regarding the duration of time.

If one can truly maintain clear and correct mindfulness, one will immediately receive the guidance of Amitābha, be entrusted within a lotus womb, and together reach the stage of non-retrogression. Is this not indeed simple and easy?
The ancients said, "Ten thousand who practice, ten thousand attain rebirth. Yet, why is it that those who recite the Buddha's name today do not necessarily attain rebirth?
(31) The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:
"If one recollects and contemplates the Buddha, one will certainly see the Buddha in the present and in the future. This is the principle of resonance and response (*yinggan*).

It is so. If ten thousand people truly invoke [the Buddha], then ten thousand people will truly receive the response. This is what is meant by "ten thousand practices leading to ten thousand deliverances.
As for those who recite the Buddha’s name with the intent to be reborn in the Pure Land, though their mouths recite the name, their minds do not rely upon the Buddha;

they continue as before to assert their own subjective views, no matter how they act. Upon hearing a word of sincere truth, they immediately find it difficult and fear it; yet upon hearing a single word of the Dharma...
If one speaks [of the practice] but treats it with ease and neglect, such recollection of the Buddha is merely a matter of following the text; it will likely not lead to rebirth in the Pure Land.

If you see what is difficult and do not fear it, and see what is easy and do not treat it with negligence, constantly seeking guidance and reflecting with urgent diligence while recollecting the Buddha according to the teachings of the ancients, their words will certainly not deceive you.

Once one has made the vow to be reborn there, it is sufficient simply to recite the Buddha’s name; why rely on cultivating various meritorious deeds, which would instead become causes for outflowing existence? (32)
In practicing the Buddha-way, both merit and wisdom are equally honored. Whether they are with-outflow (*sāsrava*) or without-outflow (*anāsrava*), these follow the inclinations of one's own mind.
One must not, because the merit of the outflowing kind is impermanent, consequently abandon the great meritorious virtue of adorning the Buddha-lands. Therefore, the *Amitābha Sūtra* states:
"One cannot attain birth in that land by means of few roots of goodness, merits, or causal conditions. Here, "roots of goodness" refers to the recitation of the Buddha’s name.
Furthermore, regarding the causes and conditions of merit and virtue, one cultivates various meritorious deeds. The "Chapter on Rebirth in Three Grades" of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states:
"One should resolve for bodhicitta, cultivate various meritorious deeds, observe the precepts and fasts, erect stupas and images, and provide food for śramaṇas."
Hang silk banners and light lamps; scatter flowers and burn incense. The *Sūtra on the Visualization of the Buddha of Infinite Life* states:

"Those who wish to be born in that land should cultivate three kinds of merit. First, filially supporting one's parents, serving teachers and elders with compassion, refraining from killing, and practicing the ten wholesome actions.
Second, receiving and upholding the Three Refuges, being fully endowed with the various precepts, and not violating dignified conduct. Third, generating the bodhi-mind..."
Focus the mind. Have deep faith in cause and effect. Read and recite the Mahāyāna sūtras. Exhort practitioners to advance.

It is further said that by giving rise to three kinds of mind, one will immediately attain rebirth. What are these three? First, the mind of utmost sincerity; second, the profound mind; third, the mind of dedication and aspiration.
Those who possess these three minds will certainly be born in that land. Such explanations as these are too numerous to be cited in full.
Students should devote their full hearts to this.
Reciting the Buddha’s name is inherently easy to practice; if it were as previously described, would it not cause people to hesitate and shrink back? (33)

The Buddha’s words do not differ; it depends solely on whether the individual can skillfully comprehend them. While innate capacities are indeed either sharp or dull, human effort may likewise be either robust or feeble.
One should simply reflect upon and strive for diligent application to the utmost of one's ability; how can one idly excuse oneself by claiming that one’s strength is insufficient?
When laypeople practice mindfulness of the Buddha, they are often entangled by worldly affairs. What skillful means is there to ensure that these do not obstruct one’s cultivation?
(34) This matter depends entirely upon the individual being skilled in managing their circumstances. If one manages them appropriately, then there will be no obstruction.
Question 35: Are the practices of *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation) and the recitation of mantras similar? Answer: They are not similar.

Mantras possess the power of majestic spiritual efficacy (*vīrya*) that is inconceivable; provided they are empowered according to the Dharma, they immediately produce a responsive resonance (*ganying*) without the need for personal investigation into the essence.
As for *nianfo*, it includes both the phenomenal and the noumenal, the nature and the characteristics, as well as the provisional and the ultimate.
There is a reality that must be attained through thorough investigation and realization; therefore, it is not analogous [to other practices].
Is the recollection of the Buddha (buddhānusmṛti) similar to the recitation of sutras? (36)

It may be said that they are similar. Why is this? For one who recites the sutras, when [the teachings] are dispersed, they constitute the various meanings of the texts, the meanings of various phrases, and the meanings of various characters;
yet when gathered together, they do not transcend the single meaning of the Buddha. As Tiantai said: "To speak of the Buddha is to encompass all.
Thus, those who now practice mindfulness of the Buddha are, in fact, mindful of the meaning of all sutras and all textual meanings.
The meaning of all phrases and the meaning of all syllables. Why is this so? Because "Buddha" (Buddha) has the meaning of "Awakening. As a sutra says:
"Supreme, wondrous awakening pervades the ten directions, giving birth to Tathāgatas; it is of the same essence as and equal to all dharmas. This is precisely that.
Regarding the practice of *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation), there are several stages of sequence and several moments that are particularly vital.

(37) The three stages of sequence are: first, *zhuanxin nianfo* (single-minded Buddha-recitation); second, *jiuxin nianfo* (investigating the mind through Buddha-recitation); and third, *yixin nianfo* (one-mind Buddha-recitation).
The three moments that are particularly vital are: first, when one is ill; second, when one is old; and third, at the time of death.
When reciting the Buddha’s name, if miscellaneous thoughts arise, one asks: "From where do these miscellaneous thoughts come?

(38) A person's body possesses but a single thought. The thought that recites the Buddha’s name is precisely this very same thing; the thought of miscellaneous thoughts is also precisely this very same thing.
It is simply because this single thought cannot be entirely devoted to the recitation of the Buddha’s name that there arises even a small portion [of distraction].
Aside from the mindfulness of the Buddha, "miscellaneous thoughts" refer to those few moments of recollection that stray outside of the Buddha;
suddenly, they catch hold of the seeds of worldly toil and affliction, slipping in at the very moment one is practicing this mindfulness of the Buddha.
How can one eliminate discursive thoughts? (Thirty-nine) They cannot be eliminated;
simply rouse your own spirit and, with this single thought, hold it entirely upon the Buddha, and discursive thoughts will naturally vanish.
Although I know this to be so, my physical and mental vigor is exhausted and weak; I am unable to cause it to cease immediately. Furthermore, what else can be done?

(40) Since the power of the Way is not yet sufficient and there is much distraction, I must gather and restrain the six sense faculties and gradually return to purity. Having no other choice, for the time being—
Employ skillful means to dispel them. When mindfulness of the Buddha arises amidst discursive thoughts, do not pay them any heed; simply continue to recite the name.
Furthermore, fix your gaze upon the Buddha image, or let the recitation be focused on the image, and naturally discursive thoughts will cease.
Practice in this manner. At first, it will indeed be effective; however, after a long time, what should one do when distracting thoughts arise again?

(41) When the inner mind becomes turbid and external objects become chaotic, the recitation of the Buddha's name loses its power, eventually becoming entangled with and disturbed by these distractions.

Do not open [your eyes]. At this time, there is no need for anxiety. Simply focus the mind on stillness and clarity, causing each syllable of the six-character Great Name to arise from mindfulness, emerge as sound from the mouth, and be heard distinctly by the ears; furthermore, let them flow forth from within that mindfulness.
Circulate and maintain this continuity so that it is never interrupted; then distracting thoughts will naturally cease.
This is truly wondrous. Yet, what can be done for those of dull faculties who are unable to do so? (42)
The Great Master Zhiyi opened the two gates of joy and aversion. For one beginning the path, it is essential to give rise to a mind of joy and aversion.

Once joy and aversion are cultivated for a lifetime, diligent effort will spontaneously arise; the inner mind, previously turbid, will gradually become clear, and external circumstances, though chaotic, will naturally dissipate.
At the time of reciting the Buddha’s name, one will experience lightness, tranquility, and bliss. If joy and aversion do not arise, one will ultimately fail to enter [the Way].

It is like this: if you do not know how to apply yourself to the practice and your recitation of the Buddha's name is filled with many distracting thoughts, you may take the six characters of "Namo Amituofo" and link them together in a continuous chain. As you recite each phrase, mark it upon the corresponding character:
the first recitation is marked on "Nan," the second on "Wu," then "A," "Mi," "Tuo," and "Fo. You must maintain this recognition without interruption.
All miscellaneous thoughts are severed; they have no place from which to arise.
Even those of superior capacity who practice mindfulness of the Buddha may still have miscellaneous thoughts. What is the method for dispelling them? (43)

The *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states: "To know that these are but empty flowers is to be without cyclic existence; there is then neither body nor mind to undergo birth and death—how much more so for those who harbor discursive thoughts?"
"You have practiced mindfulness of the Buddha for many years. Why is it that you ultimately gain no power?
(44) Having no self-mastery, you merely follow the waves and drift with the current. No matter how many years you spend thus, how can you ever gain power?"
Whether one attains rebirth or not depends on what constitutes benefit and harm (45).
To attain a single moment of resonance with Amitābha Buddha is benefit; to have even a single thread of something that cannot be let go is harm.
"Resonance" means the same as the principle that "like sounds respond to like sounds" and "like natures seek out like natures."
What is the root of pure karma? What is its cause? What is its ultimate consummation?
(46) A practitioner of pure karma should take the bodhicitta as the root, mindfulness of the Buddha as the cause, and the benefit of self and others as the ultimate consummation.

Even a single hair’s breadth of goodness may all be dedicated toward the Western Land. If one does not recite the Buddha’s name now, but merely chants sutras and dharanis, dedicating them toward the Western Land—this too would not contradict the principles of the teachings (47).

The reading and recitation of Mahāyāna sūtras are clearly stated in the scriptures; however, these constitute auxiliary practices (*sahakāri-pratyaya*). The *Amitābha-sūtra* (Contemplation Sūtra) prescribes the cultivation of visualization, while the *Amitābha-dhyāna-sūtra* (Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra) prescribes the upholding of the Name;
these are the primary practices (*mukhya-pratyaya*). To abandon the primary practice and cultivate only the auxiliary ones indicates a failure to penetrate the profound principle.

One must realize that those who cultivate visualization and uphold the Name will, even if they are reborn in a future life, attain maturity such that at the moment of death, their response to the Buddha’s grace is easily achieved. Thus one should cultivate...
As for other practitioners, I fear that their power of aspiration may become somewhat lax, and they may be diverted and led astray by others, thereby resulting in obstacles to rebirth.
Is it not necessary to observe a long fast when reciting the Buddha’s name? (48)
If one has already previously resolved upon the Bodhicitta, one would certainly not ask such a question again.
In the past, when an official asked Mazu whether he ate meat or not, Mazu replied, "To eat it is the official’s salary;
to not eat it is the official’s merit. These words are profoundly significant.
If a person who practices mindfulness of the Buddha is unable to maintain a lifelong fast, will they still attain rebirth?
(49) Generally speaking, even if one’s transgressions are slight and minor, the merit of this practice can overshadow them.

If one’s aspiration to seek rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss through mindfulness of the Buddha is most sincere and intimate, then at the moment of death, the power of the Way will surpass the power of karma, and rebirth is certain.
Within the gate of mindfulness of the Buddha, there are teachings such as "attaining rebirth while still possessing afflictions" and "the fulfillment of ten recitations.
For students, these are the greatest possible errors (50).

The Buddha does not deceive people; it is people themselves who deceive themselves. What is meant by deceiving oneself? It means relying on one's outward appearance while harboring delusions as one seeks rebirth, and thus carelessly committing karmic offenses.

One might think that because the ten recitations have been accomplished, one may proceed at will and remain negligent. How could such a person know that those who harbor delusions do not wait until the three delusions are completely severed?
As for the "ten recitations," this is said in reference to those who are extremely busy and have no leisure for many recitations. This is *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation).
People do not awaken to this principle and thus waste their lives in procrastination. At the moment of death, the power of karma overcomes the power of the Way;
alas, what can be done? Therefore, during one's daily life, one must certainly wash away evil habits and stimulate one's roots of goodness, so as not to bring about one's own ruin.
When Master Lianchi was about to pass away, he gave this instruction: "Recite the Buddha's name with sincerity; recite the Buddha's name with sincerity alone.
Therefore, there is no need to seek out or engage in doctrinal discussions. (51)
"Sincerity" (*lǎoshí*) refers to being pure, genuine, and free from delusion. It does not mean that one fails to seek understanding in order to be sincere. As the Sūtra says:

"If the Buddha-dharma were not explained by someone, even those with wisdom could not comprehend it. The world calls those who are simple and unadorned "sincere people," but if they possess no knowledge at all, they are called "dullards.
When we speak here of "sincerely reciting the Buddha’s name," it does not mean reciting like a dullard; this can be easily understood.

One knows that the six deluded false thoughts of worldly people do not abide for even a single kṣaṇa; how could one seek out a dull-witted person who possesses no knowledge at all to practice nianfo? (52)

Although he was a simpleton, when he heard it said that reciting the Buddha’s name was good, he rejoiced; knowing that reciting the Buddha’s name was good, and hearing it said that through reciting the Buddha’s name one is reborn in the Western Paradise, he rejoiced again;
knowing that through reciting the Buddha’s name one is reborn in the Western Paradise, he then simply recited the Buddha’s name with his whole being.
He recited with his whole being today, and he recited with his whole being tomorrow, continuing to recite with his whole being until the moment his life was about to end. Suddenly—
Amitābha Buddha emits light to welcome and lead them forth; with a mere snap of his fingers, they are reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Such people may be called "stupid yet not stupid.
If one were a clever person skilled at calculation, there would be nothing they could not master and nothing they would not understand;
they would be busy today and busy tomorrow. As for those whose merit extends to future generations, let us set them aside for now; they simply remain busy until the end of the year.
On the thirtieth day of the month, karmic accumulations as vast as mountains suddenly manifest before one's eyes.

At this moment, there is no plan or means to employ, and one must wait for the karmic retribution to be dispensed. Such people may be said to be "not stupid, yet stupid"—it is precisely these whom the Tathāgata calls "pitiable."
If one practices the path yet fails to advance in realization, where lies the fault?

(53) For the practitioner, there is nothing else required; it is simply a matter of extinguishing all habitual defilements. It is like polishing a mirror: when the grime is removed, the clarity remains.
All sentient beings possess various kinds of habitual tendencies, which cause them to revolve through birth and death. Therefore, recite the Buddha’s name.

This causes the mind to turn toward Great Enlightenment, so that habitual defilements are gradually eliminated: just as one who has attained the first fruit (srotāpanna) exhaustively destroys the delusions of views;

one who has attained the second fruit (sakṛdāgāmin) further destroys six grades of the delusions of thought; one who has attained the third fruit (anāgāmin) again destroys three grades of the delusions of thought;

one who has attained the fourth fruit (arhat) exhaustively destroys both the delusions of views and thought; a pratyekabuddha attenuates the habitual tendencies; and a bodhisattva of the ten stages eliminates one grade of these tendencies in each respective stage.
Ignorance, as well as the two types of awakening—the ordinary and the sublime—are likewise thus. As for severing these delusions, how could those such as ourselves possibly achieve it?
We can only seek the Buddha’s compassionate acceptance and, following his skillful means and benevolence, attain rebirth while still bearing our delusions.

However, if coarse and heavy defilements cannot be eliminated, what kind of practitioner of the Way would we be? This applies even to greed, anger, ignorance, craving, jealousy, flattery, and crookedness, and so forth.
Mechanical contrivances, deceit, fame, profit, and private attachments—all these are evil conditions that obstruct the Way. Being unable to eliminate them, I am hindered by them;
therefore, my practice fails to advance toward the ultimate state.

Though one serves teachers and stays close to spiritual friends, there is constant fear of being dragged into the fire-pit; through blind cultivation and sightless practice, there is further dread of ending up as nothing but a mere curiosity.
Having lost both hearing and reflection, on what can one rely when advancing or retreating? (54)
It goes without saying that in this degenerate age, the Dharma is weak while Māra is strong. Nevertheless, if one examines the matter with an open mind, there may well be such people in the world.
At this time, the practice of reading the sutras must not be delayed; however, one must first understand the principles of how to read them.
For instance, if a person who recites the Buddha’s name reads the sutras, they should first select the scriptures pertaining to the Pure Land gate and investigate them in detail. One must...

Comprehend the principles and penetrate the source; do not become confused by emotional attachments or biased views. Once you have clearly understood this fundamental teaching, you may then proceed to other sutras according to your mental capacity.
For example, many lay practitioners nowadays first take up a commentary on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and study it.
Although one may cultivate pure karma, if the scriptures on pure karma are instead neglected in one's mind, this is truly beneficial in nothing but harmful.
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is profound and unfathomable; the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* is plain and without marvel.
Comparing these two sūtras, their superiority and inferiority are evident. (55)

When practitioners of the Way read the Buddhist scriptures and understand their meaning, they often regard that which is profound and unfathomable as superior, while regarding that which is plain and unremarkable as inferior.
This is utterly unacceptable. In reading the scriptures and interpreting their meaning, one must seek the plain and unremarkable principle within that which is profound and unfathomable;
and within that which is plain and unremarkable, one must seek the profound and unfathomable.
Only by following this principle can one be called truly "possessing the eye.
In the "Chapter on Rebirth through the Three Grades" of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, it is stated three times that the arousal of the bodhicitta is the essential pivot for rebirth.
Why is it that contemporary masters, when instructing others, speak only of reciting the Buddha’s name and fail to mention the bodhicitta?
The Mind (56). According to the Longshu (Lung-shu) collated edition, the phrase "arousing the bodhicitta" was omitted; Yunqi corrected this.

Master Xing'an (Sheng-an) spoke of this repeatedly and composed the "Essay on Exhorting the Arousing of Bodhicitta," which is exceedingly earnest. This is from a great spiritual benefactor of the past.
In opening the Dharma-gate of Buddha-remembrance (*buddhānusmṛti*), one must take the exhortation to generate the bodhicitta as the primary task;
only then can the purport of the vast Dharma-gates be fully realized. As for those of recent times, their conduct declines day by day; as the Confucian texts say, they are not even worth counting.
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* contains extensive discourses on the five virtues and five evils and other such passages that resemble the sūtras of the Hīnayāna (57).
The sūtra states: "There are many bodhisattvas who wish to hear this sūtra but are unable to obtain it. How could this be a sūtra of the Hīnayāna?
"To rely on the letter rather than the meaning—how could this be acceptable? Since this question has been raised, I shall attempt an explanation.
It is because this sutra remains in the world for a hundred years after the Dharma has been extinguished to deliver those with whom it has a karmic connection;
yet, in these final ages, the faculties of beings become increasingly dull. Out of the Buddha’s ultimate compassion, he is like an elder who issues a solemn warning.

As for that son, his nature is dull and inferior, making him difficult to enlighten. Therefore, one should speak words that are direct and substantial, addressing him with that which he can understand.
Regarding the words of dedication, they are often said to be "for the sake of all sentient beings" or "to universally deliver all sentient beings. Such empty vows—
It is said that vows will surely be fulfilled; this is something people find difficult to believe (58).
To have the mouth but no heart may be called an empty vow; yet if one truly possesses the heart, it becomes a genuine vow, and thus it is said they "will surely" be realized.
To universally benefit those in the present and to extensively deliver those in the future—if these were to arise abruptly and in isolation, they would inevitably remain mere empty talk.
In the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, whenever the youth Sudhana visits a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), he invariably says:
"I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva path and cultivate the bodhisattva practices.
I have heard that the Holy One is well able to provide instruction; I pray that you will explain this to me. This is the first [stage of] generating the mind.
The mind is the excellent model for practice. Since one has already first resolved upon bodhicitta, all subsequent practices flow forth from that bodhicitta.
Whether it be universally benefiting sentient beings or extensively delivering them, all such acts are inspired by bodhicitta;
they are true and not false. How could there be any reason for them not to be fulfilled?
The *Amitābha Sūtra* states: "One cannot be born in that land by means of few roots of goodness, merit, or causal conditions.
Thus we know that with much one will be born there, whereas with little one will not. (59)

According to the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, regarding the three grades of rebirth, this [passage] specifically refers to the superior grade. As for the middle and lower grades, they have their own respective distinctions.
In the practice of nianfo (buddha-recitation), what is valued is holding it in mind; why necessarily utter it with the voice? (60)

Holding the Buddha in mind while reciting his name is indeed in accord with the profound intent. However, for those who recite the Buddha’s name aloud, they take the sound of the Buddha as an auxiliary condition;
this possesses the wondrous quality of benefiting both oneself and others simultaneously.
If that is so, is silent recitation permissible?
(61) When reciting the Buddha's name alone, both vocal and silent recitation are appropriate; however, when reciting in accordance with the assembly, one must certainly recite aloud.
Some say that the six-character recitation still retains the sense of taking refuge and paying homage, whereas the four-character recitation is merely the direct invocation of the name;
they consider this to be improper. Is this so, or not? (62)

This was not taught in the ancient [scriptures]. This is merely according to worldly conventional understanding and perception; however, the meaning of the name [of the Buddha] does not pertain to this.
Is there also benefit in recollecting the Buddha while in a state of torpor? (63)

To recite the Buddha’s name while in a state of dullness and lethargy is truly to recite with the mouth while the mind does not recite. You must strictly maintain self-vigilance and never allow this to become habitual.
It is commonly said that for laypeople to practice nianfo and recite sutras causes their descendants to be few; is there indeed any truth to this?
(64) To do good brings down blessings;

to do evil brings down calamity. This is an immutable principle. Now, if one brings down calamity through the practice of *nianfo* (reciting the Buddha’s name) and reciting sutras, could it be that *nianfo* and reciting sutras are themselves evil deeds? How can this principle be reconciled? Furthermore, [the family] lacks descendants.
Such people are not uncommon in this world; they are not necessarily those who practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name or the reading of sutras.
This is spoken from the perspective of worldly phenomena. If one discusses the Dharma of the Buddha, however, descendants are merely the karmic conditions formed in previous lives.

Virtuous descendants are the result of wholesome karmic conditions, while unworthy descendants are the result of unwholesome karmic conditions. All things subject to impermanence are entirely like dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows.
65. Regarding the shadow [of the Buddha], the speed or slowness of reciting the Buddha’s name, the high or low pitch of the Buddha’s voice, and the walking or sitting posture during recitation:
how should one act in accordance with the Dharma?
If the mindfulness of the Buddha is too slow, the mind will scatter and lack power; if it is too hurried, one loses composure. When neither slow nor hurried, the practice is serene and clear.
If the voice for the Buddha’s name is too high, it may injure one's vital energy; if it is too low, it easily leads to dullness and distraction.
When neither high nor low, the sound is resonant and harmonious. Within the dharma hall, when the great assembly recites the Buddha’s name, there are fixed rules for both walking and sitting.
Fragrance. If you have two or three close companions, you may practice the mindfulness of the Buddha with ease;

simply ensure that your recitation of the Buddha’s name is performed according to the Dharma, without being bound by fixed conventions, as flexibility is permissible. Generally speaking, sitting should predominate while walking should be minimal;
furthermore, one should sit more during clear and bright times, and walk more during times of dullness or distraction. This is the general principle.

Recently, during the seven-day period following the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, I observed that in the evenings they ran the incense while reciting the Buddha’s name, which they call "seizing the Western Pure Land. Is there such a practice? (66)
When I first heard this, I was involuntarily struck with great alarm. Is it possible that even the Western Regions could be plundered?
This is truly because people do not believe in the practice of nianfo (reciting the Buddha’s name), they hold it in contempt, and even those who possess faith are unwilling to practice nianfo;

all of them have been misled by such groundless talk, and consequently fail to arouse the aspiration for the Way. Furthermore, it causes many who are discerning to avoid it before it is too late. Alas!
How strange! How tragic! With the mind undistracted, seek further instruction once more (67). The moon of the mind is solitary and full;
its light swallows the myriad phenomena. When the mind is not itself the mind, from where could distraction arise? If you turn toward a second [state]...
The Gate: It is not that there are no skillful means. For example, suppose a person is deeply attached to a certain thing—perhaps lute, chess, calligraphy, or painting;
or perhaps strings, bamboo flutes, pipes, or cords. He is so intent upon this that he truly disregards his very life.
In the cold, he knows not the cold; in the heat, he knows not the heat; in weariness, he knows not weariness; in hunger, he knows not hunger. All other proper affairs are utterly cast aside.
However, if someone comes to obstruct you, the resentment is beyond words. Now, this matter of reciting the Buddha’s name to seek rebirth in the Western Land is exactly like that;
it is simply to maintain a single-mindedness without distraction.
For those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha, what illness is greatest? What illness is most frequent?
(68) In its profound stillness and numinous clarity, the mind is originally without illness. When emotions arise, wisdom is obstructed, and all manner of illnesses emerge.

Among these, biased attachments are the greatest illness, and greed is the most frequent. However, this applies not only to mindfulness of the Buddha; it is the same for all forms of cultivation. Thus, Yongming...
Master Shou composed the *Zongjing lu* (Record of the Source-Mirror) in one hundred fascicles and the *Wanshan tonggui ji* (Collection on the Convergence of Myriad Good Deeds) in six fascicles;
both are wondrous medicines for curing biased ailments.
While those who are biased toward greed are certainly foolish, I fear that even the wise may not necessarily be so. (69)

The habitual tendency toward partiality and greed—if even a worthy person possesses this, its affliction is all the more subtle; yet one should know that the persistence of strife arises precisely from such partiality.
That the Buddha-dharma has declined and withered is entirely due to its destruction by the habitual tendency toward greed. When I reflect upon this, tears involuntarily fall.
If one wishes to turn back the surging waves that have already collapsed, how can this be achieved?

(70) It depends entirely upon powerful great beings who, mindful of their profound kindness, shall all join together to lift it up. Though this unworthy person lacks merit, [I pray for your assistance].
I venture to offer my service like that of a whip-bearer.
Now, in propagating the Dharma-gate of the Buddha-Recitation, what should be taken as the primary task?
(71) Confucianism says: "In all matters, one must follow the ancients. It also says: "First, one’s character must be lofty; second, one must have a teacher and model."
Ancient ones! We who cultivate the Way within the Buddha-dharma should likewise uphold these words. We should select the ancients as our models;
even if they do not conform to the needs of the present age, what harm is there in passing our days according to conditions?
Selecting the ancients as one's model, I request to know who they were (72). In matters, seek simplicity;
if the effort is profound, the merit will surely be great. To be diffuse and follow many divergent paths is to have fame without substance. Now, within the Buddha-dharma...
As for those who are well-known to people and who also possess extensive scholarly research, there are only three:
Chan Master Yongming Shou, Grand Master Lianchi, and Dharma Master Xing’an.
Among the texts on the purification of karma, the books are numerous and voluminous; one also seeks those that are concise and easy for people to consult.
Which books are these? (73) *Yunqi Fahui* by Master Lianchi; *Miaozong Chao* by Dharma Master Zhili of Siming; and *Sheng'an Fa*... [text fragment].
The Master has authored the *Collected Works of Dharma Master Sheng’an*, all of which are essential.

His *Wanxian Tonggui Ji* (Collection on the Universal Return of All Goodness), although not exclusively dedicated to the practice of Pure Land, is nonetheless indispensable for those who cultivate Pure Land.

As for the *Zongjing Lu* (Record of the Source Mirror), its extensive prose and manifold meanings constitute the foremost great treatise on the cultivation of the path; it must not be neglected. During the Song dynasty...

The layman Wang Rixiu has the *Longshu Jingtuzhi* (Pure Land Texts of Longshu). Furthermore, the layman Peng Erlin of Wuzhong during our dynasty compiled the *Jingtu Shengxian Lu* (Records of the Sages and Worthies of the Pure Land).
Both of these works serve as authentic models for the practice of pure karma. These two laymen were practitioners of nianfo at home who maintained their cultivation with profound sincerity;
they were the pillars of this Dharma gate. Recently, I have produced a humble carving of the *Lianzong Jiuzu Zhuan* (Biographies of the Nine Patriarchs of the Lotus School).
[Omitted. I intended to provide a basis for the authentic lineage and source-currents of the Lotus School, yet the written work is so brief that it is extremely concise.
For the sake of the Dharma and for sentient beings, what should take precedence? (74)
First, one must act for oneself. Why is this? If one does not first act for oneself and bring oneself to full realization, how can one possibly act for the Dharma or for others?
Not only will one fail to serve the Dharma or others, but one will actually cause much harm to the Dharma and to people, while bringing no small amount of ruin upon oneself.
The great matter of the Buddha-Dharma is like an eighty-year-old man entering the examination hall; it is no child’s play. It must not be treated lightly.
I do not know. To like acting as a teacher for others is not necessarily out of ill intent. Why, then, would there be fault?
(75) One who likes to act as a teacher is in fact self-opinionated and self-willed; they have never attained true clarity, yet they consider themselves to be clear.
Therefore, there is a transgression.
It goes without saying that those who have left the household life and received the precepts are exempt; however, how can laymen and laywomen enter the Way? (76)

Having already generated right faith and right aspiration, one should first receive the Three Refuges. Once this practice has become mature, one should personally resolve to advance and receive the Five Precepts;
however, one must first select a qualified master of the renunciant path before seeking to receive them.

As for the Bodhisattva Precepts, those based on the ten grave and forty-eight light offenses according to the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* are precisely the characteristics of the Bodhisattva Precepts. One must...
One must personally and respectfully resolve to generate the Great Mind. By no means should one receive the Buddha’s precepts merely to follow the whims of others or to conform to their inclinations.

At this time of receiving the precepts, the most essential things are a mind of profound earnestness, a mind of reverence, and the realization that such an opportunity is difficult to encounter in a thousand lifetimes.
One must generate the great Bodhicitta; by no means should one heedlessly or lightly listen to the urging words of the moment.
The citations from scripture and ancient precedents he adduces are all statements made at inappropriate times.

That the *śikṣamāṇā* [is so defined] has been passed down erroneously from one error to another, with no one to correct it—this is truly lamentable. My unrefined and reckless words being thus are not intended to obstruct this excellent opportunity;

rather, they are meant to stimulate a superior resolve and thereby bring about this excellent opportunity. (The *śikṣamāṇā* refers to members of the female monastic community; since she is nowadays taken to mean a maiden, it is called an error.)
If one does not receive the precepts of taking refuge, can one still practice?

(77) One may indeed practice; however, one must clearly understand the reason for not receiving them. If it accords with correct principle, then it is permissible. Otherwise, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states:
"To receive and uphold the Three Refuges and be fully endowed with the various precepts is the primary cause for pure karma. Furthermore, [the author] says: "I, the unworthy one..."

There is one word [to be noted]: if a woman wishes to receive the precepts of refuge, it is not improper to invite a teacher to her home and respectfully receive them while ten seats are arranged in the hall.

This is recorded in the "Western Pure Land Synthesis" (*Xifang helun*) as part of the "Ten Essentials of the Pure Land. At the end, there is an article titled "A Record of a Dream," which describes a most extraordinary event. (7)
(18). Strange, how strange!
Let us set aside for a moment the final statement; you should bear it in mind. Zhonglang said: "I did not expect my joy to reach such an extreme.
Had I strictly maintained the precepts during my lifetime, I would not have reached this point. For the most part, it is due to..."
When both precepts and wisdom are urgent, one’s rebirth is of the highest grade. Next, when precepts are urgent [and wisdom follows], the rebirth is most stable.

If one possesses wisdom but lacks precepts, they will mostly be dragged by the power of karma and flow away into the assembly of the eight classes of ghosts and spirits; I have personally seen such people among my own kin.

My younger brother has a profound affinity for Prajñā, yet his precepts and meditative concentration are very slight. Now, if one realizes the principle but cannot give rise to precepts and concentration, that too is madness.

This is wisdom. Return to the five turbidities while you are still strong and healthy; truly awaken and truly practice, while simultaneously upholding pure vows and diligently applying skillful means.
Have compassion for all beings, and before long, you will surely attain a noble realization. Once you enter another path, it will be terrifying and fearsome.
If you are unable to maintain the precepts, there exists the "Six Fasting Days Method" of Nāgārjuna; follow and practice it. The precept against killing is especially urgent. [End of] entrustment.
I say to my fellow students: from the first day one begins to wield the carving knife, if the mouth craves savory flavors, it will be impossible to give rise to purity and tranquility.
Though one may preach the Dharma like clouds and rain, what benefit is there for the matter at hand? This, then, is true speech and reality;
this can truly be called assisting in the propagation of the Buddha’s transformation. You should take this to heart.
The *Contemplation Sūtra* states: "Recite and chant the Mahāyāna. Since Mahāyāna sūtras are extremely numerous, which sūtra should one read as essential?

(79) Regarding those who recite and chant the Mahāyāna, apart from the three sūtras [of the Lotus, Nirvāṇa, and Amitābha], the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Complete Enlightenment* (*Awakening of Faith*) are most excellent for constant recitation; the others may be followed accordingly.
It is possible through effort.
When reading the sūtras, one must understand their meaning rather than merely reciting them.
As Master Pang said in his verse: "When reading the sūtras, one must understand the meaning; understanding the meaning leads to practice. If one relies on the study of definitive meaning..."

One should immediately enter the city of Nirvāṇa. However, while reading correctly, there is no need to pause the voice to explain the meaning; during the time of recitation, one should simply focus on achieving fluency.
Wait for a moment of stillness and tranquility, then select a passage or a single sentence at a time to savor its meaning in detail, or perhaps take it up again for thorough understanding.
Investigate and synthesize these [teachings]. After a long time, a point of realization will naturally arise; this is what is meant by "understanding the meaning" (*jieyi*).
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is highly esteemed by the world; why then has it not been included among the standard recitations? (81)

Among the people of this world, those who recite and practice this sutra are found everywhere. This is likely because they have seen the *Platform Sutra*, which records the Fifth Patriarch instructing others:
"If you read the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* thoroughly, you will be able to clarify the mind and see its nature.

Yet, from ancient times to the present, though those who recite the sutra are very numerous, those who truly comprehend it in their hearts are extremely few. Why is this? It is because they do not examine it with understanding.
It is not otherwise; it is simply that you have been misled by commentaries. Even if you have moments of awakening, they are all merely intellectual speculations and not true awakening.
You do not realize that if one simply reads the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* with familiarity, one will suddenly attain understanding;
there is, after all, a point of entry. This is why the Fifth Patriarch spoke as he did. However, this meaning is not easily explained to others.
"Regarding all the sūtras, there are a great many commentators; do they all mislead people? (82) Alas! What is this you say?
Each has its own appropriate capacity; they cannot be treated as one and the same. For the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, there are the *Śītalā-vyākhyā* and the *Vyākhyā-ṭīkā*;
for the *Avataṃsaka-saṃgraha-śāstra*, [there is the commentary]; and for the *圆觉经* (*Yuánjué jīng*), there is the *Guìfēng lüèshū*. Master Guìqīng [has shone] through the ages."
This is the correct interpretation. If one becomes weary of its length and complexity, one may instead consult the *Compendium* (He Lun).
Master Li proclaimed that by initiating the first thought of the Ten Abodes, one immediately achieves perfect enlightenment; truly profound are these words!

The *Brief Commentary on the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra* (*Yuanjue jing lüeshu*) by Chan Master Guifeng is concise yet exhaustive; it is a work of supreme excellence. Other commentaries on various sutras do not approach its thoroughness.

The practice of mindfulness of the Buddha is fundamentally most excellent. Yet, if someone should unjustly treat one with hostility, or if unexpected events suddenly arise to cause provocation, it may be impossible not to give rise to a mind of anger. What can be done about this? (83)
Some awaken through mindfulness of impermanence; some blame their own invitation of evil karma; some feel compassion for the ignorance of others;
and some protect their own right mindfulness. As the verses of Hanshanzi say: "Anger is the fire within the mind."
It can burn down the forest of merit. Those who wish to practice the Bodhisattva path must endure insults and guard against anger;
truly, through such sincerity, all adverse conditions will melt away like ice and crumble like a fortress.

One practices mindfulness of the Buddha fundamentally seeking liberation. Yet, suddenly, various favorable conditions and beautiful circumstances come forward to entangle and bind one. How can this be? (84)
One must first discern that all favorable conditions and beautiful circumstances are not good things; they are merely deceivers who entrap people.
