When I compare them to Amitābha Buddha in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, they appear utterly trivial and hollow. Only then do I truly come to loathe and detest them.
What craving could there possibly be?
For one who has left the household life, if they encounter favorable conditions and auspicious circumstances, it is precisely the right time to propagate and flourish the Buddha-dharma;
this cannot be discussed in the same way as for those remaining at home. (85)
To cause the Buddha-dharma to flourish and prosper—how easy is this to speak of! Those who have left the household life with a sincere heart should reflect upon this themselves;
they should contemplate it deeply. They must settle all favorable conditions and auspicious circumstances properly, ensuring that they do not mistake cause for effect.

Laypeople engage in worldly activities and cultivate their livelihoods; now, to take refuge in the Triple Gem and practice mindfulness of the Buddha seems, I fear, inconsistent with reason. How should one proceed? (86)

This matter further depends upon each individual to skillfully manage their own circumstances. Since the conditions of people vary from one to another, it is difficult to provide a definitive statement.
Among the karmas created, taking life is the most serious; yet, if one engages in worldly activities to sustain one's livelihood, [one must exercise great care].
Within this, there is great benefit in accumulating merit and virtue; for now, let us set that aside.

Generally speaking, when one knowingly commits transgressions and evil karma accumulates, how can the mind remain at peace? It would be like abandoning a household business that has grown too vast and seeking a livelihood in something more modest;
if one could ensure that one does not fall into hunger or cold, one might as well cast off the two characters "karma-creating. Would that not be excellent? Whether poor or rich—
It rests with the mandate of Heaven; it must not be confused. The practice of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recollection) is a matter of life and death; it must not be mistaken.
Since I have been unable to achieve single-mindedness in my *nien-fo*, I beg for one more word of guidance. (87)
Whenever one practices the recitation of the Buddha’s name, it is not necessarily done without interruption throughout the six periods of the day.
Even if one recites for only a single period, it may last no more than one or two incense sticks. Even if other matters arise, one should first arrange them properly and then begin the recitation.
Once the mind is free from such concerns, one can disregard ten thousand other things. Thus, sitting upon the meditation cushion, one should rouse the spirit and hold fast.

Be diligent! Focus your single thought upon the Buddha, word by word, without allowing for even a moment’s slackness. If you do this, how could it be difficult to attain single-mindedness with these one or two sticks of incense?
I constantly follow my mindfulness of the Buddha and desire to achieve single-mindedness, yet it remains unattainable.
I beg for one more word of guidance (88).
Why do you explain this "single-mindedness" differently from the "single-mindedness" asked about previously? As for the former, it was merely...
One must disregard everything else; one cannot do without single-mindedness. This is the single-mindedness that is free from the distraction of affairs.
However, no one can avoid having affairs. When there are affairs, how can one not attend to them? To make preparations in advance is only possible for a brief moment;
how could one possibly arrange things to follow the constant flow of time? If, when affairs arise, the mind is stirred by them, then one cannot attain single-mindedness.
For such a person, there would never be a time when they attain single-mindedness; how could this possibly be reasonable?

One should know that "not making the mind dual" is also a designation for single-mindedness. What is meant by "not making the mind dual"? It means to remain as one regardless of whatever various matters may arise.

While others half-heartedly stir their thoughts to respond to circumstances or engage in planning and calculating, my mind of mindfulness of the Buddha and aspiration for birth in the Pure Land remains courageous, firm, unmoving, and unshakable—whether in the midst of affairs or in the absence of them; it neither increases nor decreases.
This is what is meant by "non-dual" mind. A non-dual mind is the single-mindedness that persists whether one is engaged in affairs or not. This is having affairs... [and yet remaining single-minded].
It is the single mind within the divided mind.
Although your previous guidance was extremely thorough and lucid, it pertained only to the single mind among many;
it did not yet reach the single mind that is without [the notion of] a single mind. Ultimately, this does not constitute a true realization of the principle of the single mind (89).
If you take the absence of a single mind to be the true realization of the principle of a single mind, you have fallen into the view of nihilism.
Do you not know that the views of existence, non-existence, both existence and non-existence, and neither existence nor non-existence are all mere conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*)?
I now pay no heed to views of existence or non-existence, views of neither existence nor non-existence, nor views of both existence and non-existence;

I simply focus on reciting the Buddha’s name to seek rebirth in the Pure Land, while simultaneously perceiving neither existence, nor non-existence, nor that which is neither existent nor non-existent.

One does not perceive either existence or non-existence; one perceives only the mind that recites the Buddha’s name with the aspiration to be reborn in the Pure Land. This mind is clearly ungraspable.
Since the innate capacities of human beings are not uniform, how can they all return together to the Right Path? (90)
Those who study the Way cannot do without a clear teacher and virtuous friends. Furthermore, one must select a master of true realization as such a teacher and friend.

As the ancient saying goes: "If you do not encounter a master at the outset, you will end up as nothing but a collection of old bones by the time you grow old. This is of vital importance for one's lifelong spiritual practice.
Is this not also a grave matter? In ancient times, when people encountered a master or a teacher of great works, they would forget their own lives to follow them;

thus, it was easy for them to return to the Right Path and their practice easily reached completion. People today treat their teachers and friends with contempt and utterly lack the heart to seek the Way.
If one’s conduct accords with theirs, they will associate and interact with them; yet if one opposes them even slightly, they distance themselves and flee. Therefore, the Right Path is obscured.
Such people are rare indeed. May the discourse on *gongfu* (spiritual cultivation) still be questioned?
Su Dongpo used to carry an image of Amitābha with him at all times; this may be called earnest. Why, then, did he not attain rebirth there? (91)
In the past, the Layman Dongpo painted a single scroll of Amitābha’s image.
When someone asked about it, he said, "This is my official passport for the Western Paradise; my aspiration to be reborn in Sukhāvatī can be seen therein.
However, when he was at the point of death, someone urged him regarding matters of the West, to which he replied, "The West is not non-existent, yet one cannot apply effort within this very place."
Consequently, he never heard of his rebirth in the Pure Land. Alas! At the very time one ought to exert effort, he instead said that effort was of no avail;
was this not a mistake on the part of the Layman? To gauge his disposition: Dongpo was a great genius, and according to Buddhist teachings, he had seen much error.
He believed that only by attaining the perfectly wondrous Dharma could one be considered a master. If it were an elder...
To truly practice the mindfulness of the Buddha—how does this differ from that of the ignorant masses? There seems to be a sense of dissatisfaction [with their practice].

Yet, as for the perfectly wondrous state, one has never fully penetrated it during ordinary times; now, at this moment, one merely struggles to arrange things, seeing only that there is no way to apply effort within.
For those who recite the Buddha’s name, rebirth at the time of death is straightforward and real; single-mindedly reciting the Buddha’s name is paramount.
Very well. If one is driven by curiosity or a desire for victory, it is what is called "failing through cleverness. The Layman Dongpo may serve as a model for this.
When a practitioner of Buddha-recitation is about to die, if they do not see auspicious signs, they may instead give rise to doubts.
How should this be addressed? (92)

Regarding auspicious signs at the time of death: one knows for oneself that the time has come; one sees lotus flowers for oneself; celestial music welcomes one into the void; and extraordinary fragrances fill the room.
These are manifestations occurring through the mutual resonance of the path and its response. Whether they are hidden or manifest cannot be fixed with certainty.
One must know that if the cause is true, the fruit will be real; there is no need for doubt. At this moment, one should simply let go of everything.
Maintain mindfulness and strive with single-minded devotion to recite the Buddha’s name. At the time of death, one’s recitation of the Buddha’s name must be intense and powerful;
if even those who have committed the ten evil deeds can attain rebirth in the Pure Land, how much more so those who have long since made vows and practiced the recitation of the Buddha’s name!
93. Can it be determined whether a practitioner of pure karma will attain rebirth in the Pure Land at the time of death?
Generally speaking, one must examine their lifelong conduct; to judge the fruit based on the cause is the fixed law.

If one were to judge based solely on the circumstances at the moment of death, there would be no need to mention it if auspicious signs appear before them. However, this must be consistent with the *Sūtras*.
As for the combination of these characters: if they are confused and disordered, even if they appear fine, they are nonetheless not so.
To speak of it in general terms, for the most part, one whose right mindfulness is clear and distinct will necessarily possess a certain air of lucidity and self-mastery, capable of being the master;
they will certainly never be lax or lacking in vigor—a state that is sometimes clear and sometimes turbid. One simply sees them casting everything aside with ease; how could this be...?
It was like the fire going out when the oil is exhausted. My unworthy teacher, the Venerable Master, truly possessed such lofty refinement at the time of his passing;
this is something I have witnessed with my own eyes.
Regarding one's lifelong conduct, there are often significant differences between its earlier and later phases, such as being virtuous at first and evil later, or evil at first and virtuous later.

How should one determine the standard? (94) Regardless of whether it was virtuous first and evil later, or evil first and virtuous later, one should take only the final stage of practice as the standard.
At the gateway of pure practice, are there demonic hindrances? (95) How could there not be demonic hindrances?

It is rare for practitioners to be misled by others; it is mostly those who mislead themselves. They do not examine themselves with a sincere heart, nor do they cultivate intimacy with the worthy and the virtuous for the sake of the Path.
Within, they harbor a disposition that conceals their faults and transgressions; without, they feign the appearance of spiritual cultivation.
This self-deception is all termed the work of Māra.
While the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha is certainly a virtuous thing, it is not appropriate for young women (96).
The single practice of cultivation is common to all sentient beings; there is no one for whom it is unsuitable.

When we speak of "all sentient beings," this includes birds and beasts, as well as those in the hells and the realm of hungry ghosts, all of whom are included therein. The Bodhisattva manifests transformation bodies according to their respective types.
They are constantly among birds and beasts, in the realms of hell and hungry ghosts, teaching and transforming sentient beings to lead them to the Buddha-way.

Is this not entirely appropriate? We who dwell within the human order—whether as men or women, as monastics or laypeople, whether old or young—all find it most appropriate to practice, and most appropriate to practice early. Why is this so?
If birds and beasts and the like possess deeply heavy karmic obstructions, it is difficult for them to practice; in the human realm, practice is easy.
To fail to practice during this time of ease would be a great pity. As for the claim that women in their youth are unsuitable for practice, this is not so.
Among the assemblies listed in the sutras, there are often those named "young girls" (*kumārikā*); are young girls not indeed youthful? Thus said the Buddha.
"It is appropriate. Yet we say it is inappropriate; can this be so? It is simply that for all practitioners—and especially for laypeople—one must manage affairs in accordance with the Dharma.
One should not allow common folk to take their own course, drifting with the waves and merely acting to no avail.
As for the single gate of Buddha-recitation, one should place the aforementioned scriptures within the home; if the women do not know how to read, the men shall explain them."
Speak thus. Contemplate its meaning according to your capacity and diligently maintain your regular devotional practices. Frequently make vows for rebirth [in the Pure Land].
If there are those of genuine virtue outside your circle, invite them to your home to deliver a discourse.

For one who truly possesses virtue, they come for the sake of the Dharma and will certainly not lead others astray in their practice. However, if you are a poor or lowly family, amidst the busyness of your livelihood...
Seize moments of leisure to recite the Buddha’s name according to one's capacity. Repeatedly make vows to seek rebirth in the Pure Land.
Whether rich or poor, noble or humble, male or female, old or young—all may recite the Buddha’s name; it is most appropriate for them to practice.
97. When reciting the Buddha’s name and chanting sutras at home, one cannot find peace and quiet, nor can one purify one's speech. How can this be remedied?
Regarding human affairs in the world, nothing is more pressing than silver and money. For example, it is like this: if this sum of silver and money could come into my hands.
Yet, before it has even reached my hands, I frequently dwell upon it; from that moment, I am no longer conscious of it and find no peace.
This is not so for those who do not dwell upon it. Now, when one recollects the Buddha and seeks rebirth in the Pure Land, one immediately feels dissatisfied and finds no peace.

The reason for this is simply that the mind which recollects the Buddha and seeks rebirth in the Pure Land does not possess the same sense of urgency as a silver coin. Were it otherwise, it would not be so.
What is the harm in occasionally recollecting [the teachings] during moments when one is not in a state of tranquility?
As for those who cannot purify their speech, if they perform Buddha-work, there is absolutely no reason for their speech to remain impure.

Now, regarding spiritual practice, if it is simply because one has not yet purified one's speech at this time, that does not prevent one from continuing to practice and recite the sutras even while the speech remains unpurified.
What is so wrong with reciting the Buddha’s name? If one’s resolve for the Way is truly courageous and one sees through it clearly, who cannot purify their speech?
The three teachings share the same source; how is its ultimate principle to be understood? Nowadays, among those practicing Buddhism while remaining laypeople, many promote [the teachings].
(98) Writings. Nowadays, those who have newly developed faith and are proficient in the written word invariably speak, upon opening their mouths, of the "three teachings sharing a single source.
However, these three teachings each have their own gateways, each has its own family laws, and each has its own ultimate principle; how could they be identical? If one reaches [the ultimate],...

Regarding the identity of principle: when Śākyamuni Buddha was first born upon the earth on the eighth day of the fourth month in the twenty-fourth year of King Zhao of the Zhou dynasty, within the palace of King Śuddhodana in the kingdom of Madhyadeśa in Central India, he immediately pointed one finger toward heaven.
Pointing a finger at the ground, he declared clearly: "In the heavens above and the earth below, I alone am the most honored.

By saying "I alone am the most honored," it should be understood that there is no one who can equal him; this reveals the ultimate principle of the Buddha—that, in truth, there is nothing that can be his peer.

This is a definitive teaching (*nītārtha*), not an interpretable teaching (*neyārtha*). If it is said that the Buddha dwells at the source, such that a thousand streams and ten thousand branches do not emerge from anything other than that single source, you should reflect deeply upon this. Only when one has returned to the place of the single source can they be called "the same.
As long as one has not reached the single source but remains merely among the thousand streams and ten thousand branches, how could this not be "different"? Why?
One may say they are the same. For now, there is no need for such prolixity. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "One gate leads to the path of wondrous adornment.

Whenever one cultivates a single gate, one must enter deeply through that very gate. Now, as you cultivate the practice of Buddha-recitation (*nien-fo*), you should enter deeply through this recitation alone;
furthermore, you must not allow other gates to intermingle with it—how much less so the three teachings? As I, the unworthy one, have once said:
The principles for study within the two teachings of Confucianism and Buddhism encounter one another from time to time;

yet, there is a distinction between the ultimate truths to which Confucianism and Buddhism return, namely, the mundane and the supramundane. This unworthy one further states that the meaning of the "three teachings sharing a single source" has never been non-existent.
You need only reach the World of Ultimate Bliss and need not speak of the three teachings here. Even ten...
Throughout the infinite worlds, and within each world’s countless gates of teaching, all are contained within the single nostril of your breath;
this is not considered extraordinary. Our Buddha truly possesses such ultimate principles, fully recorded in the various sutras, which do not exist in other books.
The three teachings share a single source; to speak thus is not harmful. Why must one labor so hard to debate this?
(99) Those outside the Yuanmen (the Original Gate) frequently pilfer the words of the Buddha to delude and confuse the people of the world; this is a great harm.

As for Confucianism and Buddhism, Buddhism has the benefit of assisting Confucianism, while Confucianism has the merit of benefiting Buddhism. Viewed with the Buddha-eye, they are like two chariots traveling side by side on separate paths.

This is indeed unimpeded. It is only those Confucians who, with good intentions, study Buddhism, first perceive the profound source of Confucian principles and then claim that the single phrase "the three teachings share the same source" implies that Buddhist principles are likewise such-and-such.

Consequently, they no longer engage in refined investigation, thereby losing the stages of progressive cultivation and ultimately remaining in ignorance; they fail to exhaustively fathom the true source of the ocean of enlightenment, leading to—
This causes superior conditions to be difficult to achieve and the further shore to remain largely empty; this is due to the error of the doctrine that the three teachings share the same source.
Therefore, I cannot help but speak of it. The "chaos" (*hundun*) of the Confucian school and the "three calamities" (*tri-kalpa-vināśa*) of Buddhism bear a faint resemblance to one another.

When the great third calamity arrives, all things are utterly destroyed, leaving nothing but vast emptiness. It is certain that even the Great Sages and Great Worthies of the Confucian tradition [would not escape].

This is not something performed by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). These are individuals at the stage of fruition who have transcended the three realms; they manifest bodies here in accordance with the various types of beings merely to transform others and deliver the world.
Since they fundamentally do not sink or perish, one cannot generally speak of them as "falling."
The essentials of the Pure Land Dharma Gate and the practice of reciting the Buddha’s name for rebirth are briefly elucidated herein.
From among these, the most refined points have been further extracted so that both the refined and the common may appreciate them, and all who possess eyes may behold them. (100)
In ordinary expositions of the Pure Land, it is often said that faith, practice, and aspiration are the most essential.
However, as I see it, the ancients brought forth the two gates of "delight" and "aversion"; these two characters, delight and aversion, are even more essential. Yet this is still not enough.
If one does not apply oneself with sincerity, then even delight and aversion are merely empty talk. Therefore, know that having understood delight and aversion, one must further add to them.
To practice with earnestness can be called the most essential among essentials; it is truly the refined core. What is meant by "rejoicing"? Rejoicing means to admire and yearn for.
To admire and yearn for the recitation of the Buddha's name, to admire and yearn for the Western Land—if one can truly admire and yearn, the mind will surely become urgent and sincere.
What is meant by "disgust" (*yàn*)? Disgust is the act of wearying detachment. One grows weary of and detaches from the Sahā world; one grows weary of and detaches from birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

If one can truly grow weary and detach, the mind will surely turn away [from worldly things]. Where there is joyful longing, there must be weary detachment; where there is weary detachment, there must be joyful longing.

There has never been one who grows weary and detaches without joyful longing, nor one who joyfully longs without weary detachment. When this joyful longing reaches its ultimate point, it is what is called "faith" (*śraddhā*).
Faith must be genuine; this is what is meant by practice. Practice must be single-minded; this is what is meant by aspiration. Aspiration must be sincere.

If one’s yearning and admiration are not extreme, and one’s revulsion and renunciation are not extreme, then even if there is faith, that faith will necessarily be shallow; even if there is practice, that practice will necessarily be superficial.

Although one may have aspirations, those aspirations will inevitably be superficial. Therefore, if one wishes to encourage others to give rise to true faith, cultivate dedicated practice, and establish genuine vows, one must first open the two gates of joy and aversion.

This causes others to reach the height of joyful longing for the matter of reciting the Buddha’s name and seeking rebirth in the Western Land, and to reach the height of weary detachment from the ocean of birth and death within this Sahā world of the five turbidities. Only then will [true faith arise].
Initiate with faith; bring it to maturity through dedicated practice; achieve it through sincere aspiration; and further spur yourself on with earnest cultivation.
For those who practice *nien-fo* in this manner, there are none who will not attain rebirth. These words are neither profound nor subtle, yet they are neither coarse nor shallow.
They are neither overly detailed nor do they contain omissions. Thus, they may be appreciated by both the refined and the common alike.
All who have eyes behold it.
The questions and answers are concluded. With a sincere heart, I dedicate the merit and reverently speak these verses:
With a heart of great compassion, I proclaim the Dharma of mindfulness of the Buddha; I look up and pray to the Honored Ones of the Triple Gem.
May your compassion protect me; by means of this glow of a firefly, may it be transformed into a lamp of wisdom to illuminate the world.
May it lead me to deep mindfulness of the Buddha, and through that mindfulness, may I aspire to be born in the Pure Land and return to deliver all sentient beings.
May I attain the stage of non-retrogression in the West and proceed until the realization of Bodhi.

all are grounded in practical reality and flow from right knowledge and right view. They dissect doubts and discern delusions, being perfectly suited to the present age.
